title: Creatures of the Ruins: Goat-Demons, Lilith and Jackals
lead: When the prophets picture a city under God's judgment, its palaces fill with wild things: jackals, ostriches, owls and hyenas, and stranger beings, the hairy se'irim ("goat-demons") and Lilith (Isaiah 13:19–22; Isaiah 34:11–15). The Hebrew names are hard to pin down, and the old translations turned some animals into monsters (the KJV's "dragons" and "satyrs") and one night spirit into a bird (the KJV's "screech owl" for Lilith).

sections.b: Two oracles in Isaiah give the fullest picture. Babylon, "the beauty of the kingdoms," will end like Sodom, and its houses will be "crammed with owls" (Isaiah 13:19–22). Edom's land will be taken over by desert owl and hedgehog, ibis and raven; "It will be a den for jackals, / a haunt of ostriches" (Isaiah 34:13), and "a goat-demon will call out to its fellow" (Isaiah 34:14). The animals mean that people are gone: what humans abandon, the wild takes back. Revelation reuses the scene for the fall of the last Babylon: "She has become a home for demons" (Revelation 18:2), and Jesus speaks of an unclean spirit that "roams through dry country, searching for a place to rest" (Matthew 12:43).

Sa'ir, "hairy one," is the ordinary word for a male goat. But in a few places it names something people worshiped or feared. Israel must stop sacrificing to the se'irim (Leviticus 17:7), and Jeroboam appointed priests "for the goat idols and for the calves he had made" (2 Chronicles 11:15); the KJV has "devils" in both, and the Greek of Leviticus has "empty things." In Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 the se'irim dance and call among the ruins; this site's Plain has "goat-demons," the KJV "satyrs" (the goat-men of Greek myth), the Greek daimonia, "demons," and the Latin pilosi, "hairy ones." The BSB has "wild goats" instead. So readers divide: real goats among the stones, or goat-shaped spirits of the waste places. The STEPBible lexicon gives "he-goat" for the ordinary word and "satyr" for these verses. The goat sent "to Azazel" in the wilderness on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:8–10) belongs to the same world of the desert as the place of what is unclean.

Lilith (lilit) is named once in the Bible: "Lilith, too, will settle there / and find herself a place to rest" (Isaiah 34:14). The STEPBible lexicon defines her as a female night demon "who haunts the desolate places of Edom," and adds that the word might name a night animal. The old translations show the puzzle: the Greek has onokentauroi, "donkey-centaurs," the Latin lamia, a child-snatching monster of legend, and the KJV "screech owl." Later Jewish lore made much of her; the Talmud warns that a man who sleeps alone in a house will be seized by Lilith (Bavli Shabbat 151b). The Bible gives her no story and no power: she is one more creature of the ruins, resting where God's judgment has emptied the land. See the note and variant on Isaiah 34:14.

sections.h: Jackals, not dragons; ostriches, not owls
sections.b: Two look-alike Hebrew words are easy to confuse. Tannim, plural of tan, are jackals, the howling animals of ruined towns (Isaiah 34:13; Jeremiah 9:11; Micah 1:8). Tannin is a different word for a great sea creature, serpent or dragon (Genesis 1:21; Isaiah 27:1). The KJV printed "dragons" for the jackals again and again (Isaiah 13:22; Isaiah 34:13; Isaiah 35:7; Isaiah 43:20; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 10:22; Jeremiah 14:6; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Job 30:29; Psalm 44:19; Micah 1:8; Malachi 1:3), and the Latin did the same in Isaiah 34:13. In the same way bat ya'anah, "daughter of the ya'anah," is the ostrich in the BSB and in this site's Plain, but "owl" in the KJV (Leviticus 11:16; Job 30:29; Isaiah 13:21); the Greek of Isaiah 13:21 made them "sirens." Job's cry reads very differently once the animals are right: "Jackals are my brothers now, / ostriches my companions" (Job 30:29). None of these verses is about dragons.
